```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"))
# Console colour carries no meaning on a rendered page. pkgdown turns it on for
# its own build, and the escape sequences then reach the reader as literal text,
# so colour is switched off here for a plain vignette render and a site build
# alike. The fixed width keeps printed output inside the documentation column.
options(cli.num_colors = 1, cli.hyperlink = FALSE, crayon.enabled = FALSE,
        width = 80)

# Figures on the package website sit on a warm off-white page in light mode and
# are inverted by pkgdown in dark mode, so an opaque background would read as a
# pale slab one way and a black plate the other. Two things paint one. The
# device
# canvas is made transparent by `dev.args` above, and theme_depictr() then
# inherits theme_minimal()'s white plot.background, which is drawn over that
# canvas, so it is cleared as each figure is printed. This is deliberately a
# vignette-level choice: theme_depictr() keeps its opaque background, which is
# what a figure saved for a paper wants.
transparent_bg <- ggplot2::theme(
  plot.background  = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
  panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA)
)
knit_print.ggplot <- function(x, ...) knitr::normal_print(x + transparent_bg)
knit_print.patchwork <- function(x, ...) knitr::normal_print(x & transparent_bg)

library(depictr)
# Every chunk that touches the fitted model is guarded on lmerTest, which imports
# lme4, so one condition covers both packages.
has_lmer   <- requireNamespace("lmerTest", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggdist <- requireNamespace("ggdist", quietly = TRUE)
```

This article works through depictr's model-result plots (coefficients, model
comparison, predicted values, interactions, random effects and
goodness-of-fit). It also covers `frequentist_bayesian_plot()`, which shows a
frequentist estimate and the Bayesian posterior distribution for the same model
on one figure.

The running example is `lexical_decision`, a crossed lexical-decision
experiment (24 participants, 40 items, 960 trials). We model reaction time on
correct trials as a function of priming `condition` (related/unrelated),
presentation `modality` (visual/auditory) and item `word_frequency`, with
crossed random intercepts for participant and item. Because the design is
counterbalanced, neither fixed factor is collinear with the item random effect.

```{r fit, eval = has_lmer}
correct <- subset(lexical_decision, accuracy == 1)
fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
  RT ~ condition + modality + word_frequency +
    (1 | participant) + (1 | item),
  data = correct
)
```

<!-- Without lmerTest the live fit is skipped. Every chunk that needs `fit` is
     guarded on the same condition, so the article still knits. -->


## Coefficient (forest) plots

`coefficient_plot()` reads the fitted mixed model through `tidy_estimates()`
and draws a horizontal point-and-interval ('forest') plot. Unrelated primes and
auditory presentation both slow responses, while more frequent words speed them
up.

```{r coef, eval = has_lmer}
coefficient_plot(
  fit, order = "ascending",
  labels = c(conditionunrelated = "Unrelated priming",
             modalityauditory = "Auditory modality",
             word_frequency = "Word frequency (Zipf)"),
  title = "Predictors of lexical-decision RT (ms)"
)
```

Coefficient names are tidied automatically. `word_frequency` becomes
`word frequency`, and a factor's coefficient is labelled with its variable and
the level compared with the reference, so `conditionunrelated` becomes
`condition: unrelated`. Pass `labels` to override any of them.

A slope per Zipf unit and a contrast between two conditions are in different
units. `standardise = TRUE` multiplies the slope of each continuous predictor by
that predictor's standard deviation, so the word-frequency slope reads as the
change in RT per SD. The two factor contrasts stay as differences in
milliseconds between conditions. A contrast already compares two groups, and its
per-SD value would depend on how evenly the trials happen to be split between
them [@gelman2008]. An interaction is scaled through its inputs in the same way.
Gelman recommends two SDs, which makes a continuous slope roughly comparable
with a binary contrast. `sd_multiple = 2` follows that convention, and the axis
label names whichever convention is used:

```{r coef-std, eval = has_lmer}
coefficient_plot(fit, standardise = TRUE, sd_multiple = 2, order = "ascending",
                 title = "Predictors of RT, word frequency per 2 SD")
```

To keep the raw units instead, including a large intercept that would
otherwise compress the slopes, set `facet = TRUE`, which gives each term its own
free-scaled panel. `frequentist_bayesian_plot()`, shown below, uses this layout
by default.

## Comparing models

`compare_models()` overlays the estimates from several models so you can see how
a coefficient moves as the specification changes. Here a reduced model without
`modality` is compared with the full model, and `model_fit_table()` summarises
their fit.

```{r compare, eval = has_lmer}
reduced <- lmerTest::lmer(
  RT ~ condition + word_frequency + (1 | participant) + (1 | item),
  data = correct
)
compare_models(Reduced = reduced, Full = fit, order = "descending")
```

```{r fit-table, eval = has_lmer}
knitr::kable(model_fit_table(Reduced = reduced, Full = fit))
```

Both models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML), the default
of `lmer()`. A REML likelihood is the likelihood of the residuals left once the
fixed effects are removed. It changes with the fixed effects, so REML criteria
cannot compare models that differ in them, as these two do.
`model_fit_table()` therefore takes AIC, BIC and the log-likelihood from a
maximum-likelihood refit, as `anova()` does for lme4 fits, and says so in a
message.

The `R2` column reads `NA` for mixed models, since no single R-squared is
standard for them. For a `glm`, the column reports the deviance R-squared
[@cameron1997], the share of the null deviance that the predictors explain.
That equals the ordinary R-squared for a Gaussian model with the identity link
and McFadden's pseudo-R-squared [@mcfadden1974] for binary logistic regression.

## Predicted values and interactions

`effects_plot()` shows what the model predicts as one predictor varies, holding
the others at typical values. It also works on the mixed model, where its
predictions use the fixed effects only (`re.form = NA`) and the band is built
from the fixed-effect design matrix and `vcov()`.

```{r effects, eval = has_lmer}
effects_plot(fit, "word_frequency",
             title = "Predicted RT across word frequency")
```

`interaction_plot()` shows how a relationship changes across a second predictor.
The lexical-decision model is additive, so we switch to `crop_yield`, whose
data-generating process contains a fertiliser-by-treatment interaction.
Fertiliser raises yield far more under the `enhanced` treatment than under
`standard`, so the slopes diverge.

```{r interaction}
crop_fit <- lm(yield ~ fertiliser * treatment + rainfall, data = crop_yield)
interaction_plot(crop_fit, "fertiliser", "treatment",
                 title = "Fertiliser x treatment interaction")
```

## Frequentist and Bayesian estimates together

Given the frequentist fit and a set of Bayesian posterior draws,
`frequentist_bayesian_plot()` shows the posterior distribution of each term as
a 'ggdist' half-eye and overlays the frequentist point and confidence interval
at the same position. The two sources take the first two colours of the
colourblind-safe palette.

The draws here are the fixed-effect posterior from a `brms` fit of the same
model (1000 draws x 4 parameters). They are stored in the package so that the
slow MCMC need not be re-run. Terms are matched by canonical label, so the
`brms` parameter names line up with the frequentist ones automatically.

```{r fbp, eval = has_lmer && has_ggdist, fig.height = 4}
draws <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "lexdec_draws.rds", package = "depictr")
)

frequentist_bayesian_plot(
  fit, draws,
  intercept = FALSE,
  note_frequentist_no_prior = TRUE,
  title = "Frequentist estimate over the full Bayesian posterior"
)
```

The frequentist confidence interval and the bulk of the Bayesian posterior fall
in the same place, but only the posterior shows the density, the skew and the
mass on either side of zero.

If `ggdist` is unavailable, the function falls back to a point-and-interval
forest plot of the two sources. When the Bayesian side is supplied as a
*summary* table instead of draws, for instance the `Estimate`, `Q2.5` and
`Q97.5` of `brms::fixef()`, it draws the familiar two-source forest plot.

## Posterior distributions on their own

`posterior_plot()` summarises any draws (posterior, bootstrap or simulation) as
a distribution per parameter. With `style = "halfeye"`, it shows the density
slab and a point-and-interval. A region of practical equivalence (ROPE) can be
shaded, and each parameter can be annotated with its probability of direction,
the posterior mass on its majority side of the reference line.

```{r posterior, eval = has_ggdist, fig.height = 4}
draws <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "lexdec_draws.rds", package = "depictr")
)
slopes <- draws[c("conditionunrelated", "modalityauditory", "word_frequency")]

posterior_plot(
  slopes, style = "halfeye", rope = c(-5, 5), pd = TRUE,
  labels = c(conditionunrelated = "condition",
             modalityauditory = "modality",
             word_frequency = "word frequency"),
  title = "Fixed-effect posteriors (ms), with ROPE and pd"
)
```

The posteriors of `word_frequency` and `conditionunrelated` lie almost entirely
on one side of zero, so their probability of direction is effectively 100%.

## Random effects

`random_effects_plot()` reads the fitted model and draws a caterpillar plot of
the conditional modes ('BLUPs'). It shows the by-item and by-participant
departures from the average, sorted and with their uncertainty, which is the
usual way to spot unusual groups.

```{r ranef, eval = has_lmer, fig.height = 6}
random_effects_plot(fit, title = "By-group departures (random intercepts)")
```

## Optimiser checks

A mixed-model fit should be stable across optimisers. `lme4::allFit()` refits the
model with every available optimiser, and `optimizer_fixef_plot()` then shows
the fixed effects side by side, one panel per term. Tight clusters mean that the
fit is stable, and scattered points would signal a fragile solution.

The package includes the `allFit()` summary for this model, so we can plot it
without re-running the slow refits. The plot accepts a tidy data frame of
optimiser-by-term values, which we take from the stored summary.

```{r optim, fig.height = 4.5}
af <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "allfit_lexdec.rds", package = "depictr"))
fx <- af$fixef    # optimisers x fixed effects
opt_long <- data.frame(
  optimizer = rep(rownames(fx), times = ncol(fx)),
  term      = rep(colnames(fx), each = nrow(fx)),
  value     = as.vector(fx)
)

optimizer_fixef_plot(
  opt_long, title = "Fixed effects across optimisers",
  labels = c(conditionunrelated = "condition",
             modalityauditory = "modality",
             word_frequency = "word frequency")
)
```

The points coincide within each panel, so every optimiser reaches the same
estimate for each term and this fit is stable.

## A one-figure model report

`model_report()` composes the coefficients, the effect of a focal predictor,
residuals against fitted values and a Q-Q plot into a single figure, with a
subtitle of fit statistics, for a quick review or a report appendix. It works
on `lm` and `glm` models, and a `glm` gets the binned-residual and
quantile-residual panels of `residual_diagnostics_plot()`. Here we use the
crop-yield model.

```{r report, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
full <- lm(yield ~ rainfall + fertiliser + soil_ph + treatment,
           data = crop_yield)
model_report(full, title = "Crop-yield model")
```
